name: Managing Your Position
question: How much capital and time does it deserve, and how do I leave?
intro: Set exposure limits, require evidence before adding, harvest deliberately, and reassess the next decision.

lessons.title: Choose the container
lessons.question: What exposure and holding time fit this opportunity?
lessons.definition: The container is your planned capital, time, tolerance for volatility, adds, and remaining exposure.
lessons.why: An interesting narrative does not determine how much you can afford to lose or realistically exit.
checks: Loss budget and total exposure
Expected attention duration and reassessment conditions
Current executable quotes for the intended size
lessons.healthy: Exposure fits both the plan and current exit conditions.
lessons.dangerous: A brief attention burst becomes an unplanned long hold.
lessons.mistake: Treating reported liquidity as a safe position-size formula.
lessons.takeaway: Plan the exposure before becoming attached to it.
example: A trader expects a short catalyst-driven burst.
Attention fades, but the trader extends the hold indefinitely.
The longer duration needs a new case, not a new label.
lessons.external: Record your budget and execution plan separately. Reported liquidity is context; obtain current buy and sell quotes for your actual size.
lessons.deeper: The source's attention magnitude × durability expression is a planning analogy, not a sizing equation. Attention, personal loss tolerance, portfolio exposure, and executable liquidity all matter. Plan → initial exposure → evidence review → harvest or reduction → fresh reassessment is a workflow, not an instruction to take every stage.

lessons.title: Opportunity vs portfolio risk
lessons.question: What happens to the whole portfolio if this fails?
lessons.definition: Position risk is the loss on one trade. Portfolio risk includes its size and the exposure that can fail alongside it.
lessons.why: Possible large upside does not compensate for exposure that threatens the entire portfolio.
checks: Loss if the position becomes worthless
Leverage and obligations beyond the initial capital
Other positions exposed to the same failure
lessons.healthy: Failure remains tolerable at portfolio level.
lessons.dangerous: An imagined multiple becomes permission for unlimited exposure.
lessons.mistake: Treating potential upside as its probability.
lessons.takeaway: A possible 10x does not justify full exposure.
example: A $1,000 portfolio holds a $100 unlevered position.
If it becomes worthless, $900 remains, ignoring costs and other changes.
This illustrates loss exposure; 10% is not a sizing recommendation.
lessons.external: Use a complete portfolio record, including leverage and linked obligations. Meme Fast does not calculate your maximum portfolio loss.
lessons.deeper: In the same simplified example, a $100 position appreciating to $1,000 leaves a $1,900 portfolio when the other $900 is unchanged. The position gained $900; the portfolio gained 90%, before costs. Such arithmetic says nothing about the chance of that outcome or whether the displayed valuation can be sold.

lessons.title: Scout, then earn promotion
lessons.question: What new evidence would justify more exposure?
lessons.definition: A scout is limited initial exposure within a plan. Promotion means considering more exposure after independent evidence improves.
lessons.why: Price movement alone does not answer whether the case or execution conditions improved.
checks: Current hygiene and unresolved critical evidence
Independent demand and thesis confirmation
Total exposure and executable cost after an add
lessons.healthy: A proposed add has fresh evidence and fits the original limits.
lessons.dangerous: Excitement or fear of missing out drives promotion.
lessons.mistake: Buying a position to replace the necessary due diligence.
lessons.takeaway: Promotion needs evidence, not just a moving price.
example: Price rises after a limited initial entry.
Independent buyers and liquidity improve, while hygiene is rechecked.
Consider the new evidence alongside the remaining budget.
evidence: Compare sampled buyer activity and selling. Verify current hygiene, broader thesis evidence, and execution quotes separately.
lessons.deeper: Market confirmation can include persistent buyers, absorption, and liquidity changes. Thesis confirmation can include credible attention, a verified catalyst, or product evidence. Correlated copies of the same claim are not independent confirmation. Small size cannot fix a failed hygiene gate or guarantee an easy exit.

lessons.title: Adding up or down
lessons.question: Is the reason to add stronger than the price change?
lessons.definition: Averaging changes your entry cost and total exposure. Its rationale depends on evidence and limits, not direction alone.
lessons.why: A cheaper price can accompany a weaker thesis; a higher price can accompany better information.
checks: What improved independently of price
Whether the original invalidation still holds
New total exposure, exit depth, and risk budget
lessons.healthy: The add survives a fresh review of evidence and cost.
lessons.dangerous: A falling price becomes the entire reason to buy more.
lessons.mistake: Improving the average while worsening portfolio risk.
example: Price falls below the first entry.
The trader wants to add, but buyers and liquidity are weakening.
A lower average does not repair the deteriorating case.
evidence: Review observed structure and reported liquidity, then check sampled flow in Inspect. These do not determine your add size or execution price.
lessons.deeper: Neither averaging up nor averaging down is automatically justified. Review location, thesis, current hygiene, invalidation, and fresh risk together. A technically attractive area can still fail; a stronger thesis can still be too expensive or too illiquid for the intended order.

lessons.title: Harvest & residual exposure
lessons.question: After the move, how much risk should remain?
lessons.definition: Harvesting realizes part or all of a position. A runner is deliberately retained exposure with its own limits.
lessons.why: A chart gain is not realized capital until a sale executes.
checks: Actual proceeds after execution costs
Remaining position value and exit capacity
Why any retained exposure still belongs in the plan
lessons.healthy: A partial sale reduces exposure and the remainder has clear conditions.
lessons.dangerous: Leftover inventory becomes an indefinite hold without reassessment.
lessons.mistake: Calling the remainder risk-free after recovering the initial spend.
lessons.takeaway: A runner is still capital at risk.
example: A trader buys 100 units for $100, ignoring costs.
Selling 50 units for $150 realizes $100 profit on their $50 cost basis.
The remaining 50 units still have value that can be lost.
lessons.external: Use actual fills, costs, remaining inventory, and current sell quotes. Meme Fast does not execute harvesting or reconcile your realized profit.
lessons.deeper: Choose full exit, partial reduction, or residual exposure using current evidence and the plan. Recovering original capital is a cash-flow milestone, not the realized-profit calculation. Cost basis methods and taxes depend on applicable accounting rules; this example uses one purchase lot and excludes costs.

lessons.title: Reset the mission
lessons.question: Would you buy this now if you had never owned it?
lessons.definition: A mission reset treats re-entry or fresh capital as a new decision after a meaningful exit or harvest.
lessons.why: A previous win cannot justify the next trade's risk.
checks: Current thesis and hygiene
Remaining exposure and fresh-capital budget
New entry conditions and invalidation
lessons.healthy: The new decision stands on current evidence.
lessons.dangerous: Earlier profit is used as permission to ignore new risk.
lessons.mistake: Rebuying because the previous exit feels wrong.
example: A trader exits after the planned expansion.
Price rises again, creating an urge to return.
The old win does not answer the new entry checklist.
lessons.external: Keep a decision journal with the previous exit, current evidence, remaining exposure, and new invalidation. A saved token is not a re-entry signal.
lessons.deeper: A partial harvest does not erase the remaining position: include it in the new budget. The source calls the first cycle complete after a meaningful harvest to create a decision boundary. That boundary is a planning convention, not a requirement to close or rebuy.

lessons.title: Break the attachment
lessons.question: Are you managing evidence or protecting an old story?
lessons.definition: Entanglement happens when prior profit, loss, entry price, or missed upside controls the next decision.
lessons.why: Renaming a failed trade as an investment can hide unchanged risks.
checks: Current evidence versus the original story
Why the holding period has changed
Whether the same decision makes sense without trade history
lessons.healthy: Longer exposure has a renewed case and explicit limits.
lessons.dangerous: Avoiding a loss becomes the reason to stay.
lessons.mistake: Using conviction to describe refusal to reassess.
lessons.takeaway: An old entry does not decide today's exposure.
example: A short trade loses its original catalyst.
The trader relabels it a long investment to avoid reassessing.
The label changes; the evidence has not improved.
lessons.external: Compare your current decision with a written thesis and time horizon. Your trade history and emotional reasons need a separate journal.
lessons.deeper: Selling and immediately rebuying, chasing missed upside, and trying to recover a loss can all reflect attachment. A longer horizon needs an independently supported thesis, liquidity assessment, and exposure plan. A profitable outcome alone does not validate an emotionally driven process.

lessons.title: Attention & holding time
lessons.question: Has the reason to stay survived the first burst?
lessons.definition: Attention can appear, burst, persist, plateau, renew, or fade. Holding time should be reassessed as that evidence changes.
lessons.why: Loud discussion can persist while fresh participation weakens.
checks: Credible attention across comparable periods
Whether attention converts into observed buyers
A verified reason for renewal after the catalyst
lessons.healthy: Continued exposure has current evidence and review conditions.
lessons.dangerous: Old excitement replaces a new reason to stay.
lessons.mistake: Treating lifecycle stages as a countdown or automatic signal.
lessons.takeaway: Time in the trade needs reassessment.
example: A token's first attention burst attracts buyers.
Mentions remain high, but fresh buyer activity slows.
Review the remaining exposure instead of assuming persistence.
evidence: Compare observed attention and verify sampled participation in Inspect. Mentions do not measure capital or certify an attention stage.
lessons.deeper: The Token Attention Life Cycle is a research lens. Stages can repeat or be skipped; renewal is a possible extension, not a promised recovery. A completed migration or listing can alter the reason to buy without ensuring continuation or failure. Read the wider meta separately: Emergence → Expansion → Saturation → Rotation. Attention duration informs review; it does not calculate an optimal holding period.
framework: Token: Emergence → Acceleration → Expansion → Maturity → Decline → Exhaustion.

lessons.title: Match the evidence to the market
lessons.question: Is there enough history to read structure?
lessons.definition: Early markets often provide limited history. Later markets may offer more structure, venues, and broader market connections.
lessons.why: The evidence needed to manage exposure changes as the trading environment develops.
checks: Early move: buyer activity, absorption, and current hygiene
Later move: base, supply zones, and confirming flow
Venue liquidity, broader market context, and execution quality
lessons.healthy: Available history and market conditions guide the investigation.
lessons.dangerous: A listing or chart level is treated as safety or prediction.
lessons.mistake: Buying a Fibonacci level without demand evidence.
lessons.takeaway: Structure provides context; current behavior still matters.
example: A token retraces into a previously marked area.
Selling continues and renewed buyers are not evident.
The reference area alone does not confirm a new expansion.
evidence: Review observed price structure and reported liquidity, then use Inspect for flow. Meme Fast does not certify venue safety or a Fibonacci entry.
lessons.deeper: 202A emphasizes early demand and launch mechanics; 202B adds historical structure and holder rotation. These lenses overlap. The source's 0.5 and 0.618 retracements are optional reference areas, not validated predictions. More venues can add arbitrage, order books, funding, and market beta; maturity does not guarantee liquidity, transparency, or lower risk.

lessons.title: Portfolio limits & concentration
lessons.question: Are several tickers really the same exposure?
lessons.definition: Portfolio limits bound total exposure, new capital, correlated positions, active decisions, and losses.
lessons.why: Several tokens can fail together if they depend on the same chain, narrative, or liquidity source.
checks: Total exposure by token, theme, chain, and venue
Fresh-capital limits and concentration after appreciation
Loss limits and how many positions you can monitor
lessons.healthy: Limits are written and reviewed as positions change.
lessons.dangerous: Repeated small entries or winning adds bypass the total budget.
lessons.takeaway: Different tickers do not guarantee different risks.
example: Five positions all depend on one chain narrative.
That narrative weakens and liquidity deteriorates together.
Five names did not provide five independent exposures.
lessons.external: Keep a full portfolio ledger and group shared risks. Watchlist organizes tokens; it does not measure your holdings, enforce loss limits, or identify all correlations.
lessons.deeper: Fresh-capital concentration comes from new purchases; appreciation concentration comes from rising value. The origins differ, but both leave present capital exposed. Review concentration without assuming appreciation requires selling or licenses more buying. Include cumulative discovery losses, current exit capacity, and monitoring limits in the plan. A personal loss-limit rule needs an explicit action when reached.

lessons.title: Measure the net result
lessons.question: Did the portfolio improve after costs and failed trades?
lessons.definition: The result combines realized net profit and unrealized profit or loss on remaining exposure, with costs counted once.
lessons.why: Peak chart values and famous winners omit what was actually captured and what other trades lost.
checks: Actual fills, cost basis, and complete trade history
Remaining inventory valued consistently and realistically
Fees, external cash flows, and all losing trades
lessons.healthy: The ledger reconciles to portfolio value and cash movements.
lessons.dangerous: Full remaining value is counted as profit, or costs are deducted twice.
lessons.mistake: Judging the process only by a visible winning token.
lessons.takeaway: Score the portfolio, not the chart's highest print.
example: Buy 100 units for $100; sell 50 for $150, ignoring costs.
Realized profit is $100. At $3, the remainder has $100 unrealized profit.
Total profit is $200; its $150 remaining value is not all profit.
lessons.external: Reconcile a complete position ledger. Meme Fast's market displays are not your realized P&L, tax record, or executable liquidation value.
lessons.deeper: For a period with a consistent valuation method: ending portfolio value + withdrawals − deposits − starting portfolio value gives monetary profit. A percentage return with timed cash flows needs an appropriate return method. Actual fill prices already reflect execution effects; do not subtract slippage again from fill-based P&L. Include fees once, realized losses, failed tokens, and uncertainty in remaining valuations. Accounting profit is separate from after-tax results.

principle: Do not marry the position. Marry the net return. Reassess your exposure as buyers, dev incentives, and executable conditions change.
